title: Associative Arrays: Key‑Value Stores 🗝️
description: Map keys to values with `declare -A`. Perfect for lookups and dictionaries.

slides.title: Beyond Numbers: Named Keys 🔑
slides.content:
## Associative Arrays (Bash 4+)

An **associative array** (like a dictionary or map) uses strings as indices instead of numbers.

You must explicitly declare it: `declare -A mydict`.

Then assign: `mydict[key]=value`.

Access: `${mydict[key]}`.

slides.title: Create and Access
slides.codeSnippet:
declare -A user_name
user_name[alice]="Alice Smith"
user_name[bob]="Bob Jones"
echo "${user_name[alice]}"

quizData.question: Which command declares an associative array named `capitals`?
quizData.explanation: `declare -A` creates an associative array; `-a` is for indexed.

slides.title: Getting Keys and Values 🗂️
slides.content:
## Useful Expansions

- All values: `"${array[@]}"`
- All keys: `"${!array[@]}"`
- Number of elements: `${#array[@]}`

These work just like indexed arrays. Use `"${!array[@]}"` to iterate over keys.

slides.title: Iterate Over an Associative Array
slides.codeSnippet:
declare -A capitals=([France]=Paris [Japan]=Tokyo)
for country in "${!capitals[@]}"; do
  echo "$country -> ${capitals[$country]}"
done

quizData.question: To get all keys of an associative array, use `"${___array[@]}"`
quizData.explanation: Prefixing the array name with `!` expands to the list of keys.

slides.title: Initialising with Compound Assignment 🧪
slides.content:
## All in One Line

You can assign many key‑value pairs at once:
```bash
declare -A countries=(
  [USA]="Washington"
  [UK]="London"
)
```
Or on a single line: `declare -A arr=([key1]=val1 [key2]=val2)`.

slides.title: ⚠️ Bash Version
slides.content: Associative arrays require Bash 4.0+. If you target macOS, note the default Bash is 3.2; install a newer version or use zsh.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use associative arrays for configuration management: load key=value pairs from a file into an array for quick lookups.
